P1.evidence: No setter notes to read back — the lead came from an inbound application and no setter is named — though the rep did open on a personal detail from a previous contact, asking whether the wife's car was sorted, which does the same job of making the prospect feel seen. Frame remains three-part. Agreement asked and given. The open question ran and was then improved on: 'Realistic goals or what I really want?' / 'What you want. Be as unrealistic as possible and we'll see if it works' — which unlocked the whole first ten minutes.

P2.evidence: Weight was asked directly ('what do you currently weigh?' — 210) with height and age established in dialogue. The injury probe ran well and produced both shoulder surgeries with timing, the 50-year-old knee injury, the recent fall and the flexibility problem. Current training was fully mapped: 10-20,000 steps a day, kayaking, swimming, YMCA. Results from past attempts were elicited by a good question — 'why didn't you just start that again?' — producing the pre-pandemic drop to 170. Hereditary health came out through the longevity thread. But current day-to-day diet was never actually asked, which is a strange omission on a 50 lb fat-loss goal; what surfaced was a historical protocol plus a gluten intolerance the prospect raised himself. Sleep was volunteered in his opening sentence ('I need more sleep') and never followed up. Energy was never asked. Occupation was never asked at all.

P3.evidence: The strongest goals phase in the batch. The unrealistic-goals invitation produced everything at once — 160 lb, the 135 lb dream, the six-pack as byproduct. The can't-do-now check produced kayaking, swimming a mile, a marathon, archery. The bridge question was well built: 'there are so many 60, 70, 75-year-olds who say it comes with the age and don't take action. Why do you feel like for you, it's so important?' — which produced the three futures (the farm, travelling, and not being fat for 30 years given a family that lives into its 90s). Best of all, the impact question was asked three separate times: the prospect said 'I'm not even sure what you're asking' and the rep rephrased twice rather than moving on, eventually reaching the daughters and the two grandsons. Only the reflect-back is soft — accurate summaries, but no 'this isn't really about the weight' turn.

P4.evidence: Excellent and genuinely challenging. Past attempts surfaced (the pre-pandemic juice cleanse and elimination diet, and the abandoned YMCA weights circuit), what happened surfaced (down to 170; the circuit 'was like working in the fast food industry, there was no joy'), and the rep pressed properly on why it stopped: 'why didn't you just start that again? Why haven't you done it yet?' and then refused the first excuse — 'But you haven't yet' and 'Would it have been absolutely impossible to follow the nutrition already during that time?' and 'What's going to stop you from, in a couple of months, life gets busy again, and you just throw it to the side?' The prospect named the gap in his own words twice: 'I keep finding excuses not to start' and the joy criterion, 'if I'm not finding joy in it, I'm not going to do it.' P4f is partial only because the specific reframe was never made — this man already owns a diet protocol that provably worked and had free access to a nutritionist, and nobody said out loud that the information was never the problem.

P5.evidence: The settle question ran almost verbatim — 'are you willing to settle with it not changing because you haven't actually put in the right efforts?' — and then failed in an interesting way. The prospect answered with a five-minute philosophical monologue about joy, professional musicianship and being told he could not succeed, which never engaged the question at all. The rep summarised it charitably ('sounds like you're not willing to settle for something that you don't like') and moved on. The urgency was never established. The consequence material was there — a man who wants to live past 100, whose family reaches their 90s, who fell over on a walk three weeks ago — and the two-year picture was never drawn. No line in the sand was ever requested.

P6.evidence: The commitment was asserted rather than obtained: 'it sounds like when we begin, you are going to take it serious, right?' answered 'Right', and later 'it sounds like you feel like it's a good fit. I don't know if that's correct?' answered 'Yes.' The go-all-in question was never asked. More importantly, the prospect had left an explicit, unresolved condition on the table twenty minutes earlier — 'I really don't know if this particular activity is going to fulfill me' — and it was never converted into a yes before pricing. Given that joy is the single criterion he told the rep governs everything he sustains, that was the yes that mattered and it was never secured.

P11.evidence: Explicit no on the call. Payment and onboarding were never reachable.

objection_plays.detail: Isolation ran twice and ran well — 'out of the finances, you feel like, yes, I want to do this, or not really?' produced 'If I could afford it, yes, I would do this', which is exactly the answer the play is designed to surface. The budget-range question was then asked twice and produced the decisive number: '30, 40 a month'. Nothing else ran — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments, and no payment plan, even though the prospect raised payment plans himself ('payment plans and things like that, the big number is I don't get $1,000 a month'). Scored partial rather than miss because once a $30-40/month expectation is on the table, working a financial picture toward $6,000 would have been dishonest rather than diligent. The rep read that correctly.

The strongest instance in the whole batch of the known script gap around a cheaper alternative that genuinely worked — and here the alternative is free and proven. He has a YMCA membership he can use at no cost, an ex-student who is a nutritionist and advises him for nothing, and a dietary protocol he has personally run to a 170 lb result. He stated the conclusion himself: 'there are other ways that I can do things that's not going to cost me $6,000 and I can get healthy.' The rep's reply was a differentiation claim — 'for 50 a month, you're never going to find something that's actually customized to you' — which does not answer why customisation is worth 150 times the alternative to a man whose uncustomised approach already worked. There is no play for this and it decided the call.

A thirty-fold expectation gap, which is a qualification failure rather than an objection. The prospect expected 'any kind of a membership where it's 30, 40 a month' and his wife had pre-framed it as 'you're not going to spend very much'. No setter is named on this call and no price framing had been done. The rep handled the moment with integrity — refused to discount, said plainly 'Trevor is definitely not the cheapest, you're going to be able to find cheaper things', qualified out with 'if you're looking to spend maybe a hundred max, then this is definitely not for you', and directed him to free content. That is the right behaviour and the reason this scores partial rather than miss. The failure sits upstream, in whatever put a $30-a-month buyer on a $6,000 closing call.

'Obviously, I have to run it by her as well', plus the wife having pre-framed the spend downward and separately dismissing his gluten intolerance as psychosomatic. No OB move ran. It was arguably moot by the time it surfaced, since the price gap had already ended the call, but the wife was an active negative influence throughout and was never engaged with — including earlier, when she was raised as doubting his dietary self-knowledge.
No think-about-it. He decided on the call and said so twice.
No timing objection. He volunteered that his hours have dropped and that this is the right moment — 'I really got to get started'.

No fear or doubt about his ability. He did carry an unresolved doubt about whether the programme would be fulfilling — 'I really don't know if this particular activity is going to fulfill me' — but that is a fit question, and it belonged in Phase 6 rather than here.

notes: Phases 3 and 4 were the best work in this batch — the unrealistic-goals opener, three attempts at the impact question when the prospect did not understand it, and real refusal to accept the first excuse. All of it was spent on someone who arrived expecting to pay $30 a month. The lesson is not for the closer, it is for whoever routed this lead: no setter is attached to this call and no price framing happened, and fifty-three minutes went into a prospect who could never buy. Two coaching points that still stand. When the settle question produced a philosophical monologue instead of an answer, the rep accepted it and lost the urgency; ask it again. And the prospect said outright that he only sustains what brings him joy, then flagged that he did not know whether this would fulfil him — that doubt was never resolved into a yes before the price was quoted, and it was the only yes that mattered.
